Antarctic land ice is the ice which has accumulated over thousands of years on the Antarctica landmass itself through snowfall. This land ice therefore is actually stored ocean water that once fell as precipitation. Sea ice in Antarctica is quite different as it is ice which forms in salt water primarily during the winter months. When land ice melts and flows into the oceans global sea levels rise on average; when sea ice melts sea levels do not change measurably.

In Antarctica, sea ice grows quite extensively during winter but nearly completely melts away during the summer (Figure 1). That is where the important difference between Antarctic and Arctic sea ice exists as much of the Arctic's sea ice lasts all the year round. During the winter months it increases and before decreasing during the summer months, but an ice cover does in fact remain in the North which includes quite a bit of ice from previous years. When Arctic sea ice increasingly melts, more sunlight is absorbed by the oceans whereas Antarctic sea ice normally melts each summer leaving the earth's energy balance largely unchanged.

Hey there, I am the one behind the container layout of Voat.

The container has been put in place because it solves a few things. Firstly, while it may seem like it doesn't make sense in an age of widescreens, viewing text-based websites themselves on a widescreen doesn't make sense. It's the same reason books are portrait and not landscape oriented. So we then have the problem of whitespace, since it wouldn't make sense to make the text extend all the way to the edges of the screen (readability is first priority). Unfortunately, without a double- or triple-column layout, whitespace will be inevitable.

The container aims to displace all of the whitespace from the random places on the page into a few centralized places -- the sides. This way the content is always in the middle and doesn't really affect scrolling times. People aren't just using containers just because it's in style, these reasons are partly why it's a popular layout.

The container has the disadvantage of partially cutting off some comment threads, but it's a necessary downside in order to help solve the whitespace issue. The problem is easily solved by clicking the "permalink" button. Sites like reddit have a "continue this thread" button to solve it.

  1. You're right; human vision is landscape orientated. You're also right that that's why landscape is the best orientation for most videos and movies. However, motion videos/perception and text are apples and oranges. They're not comparable. In videos, backgrounds are important for immersion, so they serve an important purpose even though they're almost always not in focus. The focus point also jumps around throughout the frame, as the viewer looks at different objects in different places.

    With text, that doesn't happen. There is no background, nor need for one. The focus point generally follows a systematic motion as the eyes follow the words. It's different, so we need to treat it differently, and build a layout that optimizes the comfort and accessibility of that systematic motion. Unfortunately, the eyes are pretty strict on how they like their text. The font shouldn't be too big or small; the lines shouldn't be too far apart or close together; and the length the line reaches until it wraps shouldn't be too short or long.

    Lucky for us, books have been around for a very, very long time. At this point in time, we have a good idea what the best format for doing text. A legible font, a good middle-ground font size, a line width of around 60-90 characters, and line spacing that's just wide enough so the reader doesn't lose their place. Even Reddit obeys these laws, which brings up your second point:

Searching for the Algorithms Underlying Life

This reminds me of an article that I recently read in Nature entitled 'The Physics of Life'. It described the quest to describe the properties of 'active matter' ie life and other self-organizing systems via simpler physical models. The gist of the whole thing is that the theories which apply to a range of things from microtubules to flocks of birds can be described by simple interactions of neighbouring 'items' that result in collective behavior. The thing to note is that it was a decade or more from the time when this sort of model was first put forward by a Hungarian researcher whose name escapes me to the first experimental test of the subject. It has advanced since then, but it has a long, long way to go before it becomes what one might describe as "mature". In this case I foresee a further stumbling block. Computer science can be even more resistant to reality than theoretical physics. There is great potential to create elaborate programs that describe 'nothing' but look beautiful to the creator and the admirers. It's interesting, but I have my doubts.
